segments.title: Britain calls in a naval attache as Graf Spee reaches Montevideo
segments.body: On 14 December 1939, Captain McCall was called in as Graf Spee entered Montevideo harbor. British budgets in the 1930s did not cover naval representatives in every port where they might be needed, so the crisis required a naval attache to be dispatched. Eugen Millington-Drake's diplomatic preparations may have begun before the ship anchored. The apparent speed and organisation of the response are the basis for that inference.

evidence.note: McCall is dispatched because budgets do not permit naval representation in every port. Advance preparation by Millington-Drake is suggested from the response's speed and organisation, not established as a fact.

segments.summary: Captain McCall's dispatch illustrates how Britain's limited naval representation overseas shaped its response to Admiral Graf Spee's arrival in Montevideo.

segments.title: Millington-Drake's long relationships give Britain an edge
segments.body: Eugen Millington-Drake and the Uruguayan foreign minister had known each other for years and dealt with one another in an almost familial way. Long service across South America meant that officials he had met at the beginning of their careers now held senior posts. Britain could draw on that accumulated trust and access as Graf Spee sought refuge. Relationships built long before the crisis gave Britain an immediate advantage in a neutral port.

evidence.note: Millington-Drake's longstanding relationships across South America gave Britain an immediate diplomatic advantage in Montevideo.

segments.summary: Years of personal and professional relationships in South America gave British ambassador Eugen Millington-Drake unusual access to senior Uruguayan officials.

segments.title: Diplomatic protocol and the noon meeting in Montevideo
segments.body: In the film, the meeting appears to happen almost immediately after Graf Spee enters harbor. The actual interview took place at noon on 14 December, with time allowed for diplomatic appointments and courtesies. Britain's naval predominance and the apparent military strength of Britain and France in 1939 did not entitle their representatives to demand an immediate audience. Even under wartime pressure, turning up uninvited at Uruguay's foreign minister's residence would have breached diplomatic protocol.

evidence.note: The film's immediate meeting is contrasted with the noon interview. Appointments and diplomatic courtesies still constrained British and French representatives despite their countries' apparent power in 1939.

segments.summary: The film compresses the timing of the diplomatic meeting; in Montevideo, even representatives of major powers still had to arrange appointments.

segments.title: Britain first presses Uruguay to expel Graf Spee
segments.body: On 14 December, Eugen Millington-Drake's immediate aim was to have Graf Spee expelled from Montevideo as quickly as possible. He asked whether Uruguay possessed the force to carry out such a decision. His reasoning assumed that the Royal Navy force outside had already inflicted a heavy beating on the German cruiser and was strong enough to finish the job. Expulsion would, in his view, send Graf Spee straight into that force's waiting arms.

evidence.note: Millington-Drake asks whether Uruguay can enforce expulsion and assumes the Royal Navy force outside can finish the action against Graf Spee.

segments.summary: Eugen Millington-Drake sought Graf Spee's expulsion because he assumed the Royal Navy could finish the battle outside Montevideo harbor.

segments.title: Harwood asks diplomats to hold Graf Spee until Cumberland arrives
segments.body: Henry Harwood was asking for Graf Spee to stay in port while Millington-Drake was trying to have her expelled. Harwood had a force outside, but he could not be certain of success and knew that more ships were on the way. Diplomatic delay would let those reinforcements arrive. For Graf Spee, the faster she could return to sea, the better her opportunity to escape. In this assessment, HMS Cumberland's arrival effectively closed that opportunity, although those aboard Graf Spee did not recognise the danger.

evidence.note: Harwood asks for delay while reinforcements approach. The subsequent assessment argues that a quick departure offered Graf Spee her best chance and that Cumberland's arrival closed it.

segments.summary: Harwood asked for Graf Spee to remain in Montevideo while reinforcements approached, directly opposing the ambassador's push for expulsion.

segments.title: Montevideo's principal dockyard refuses to support Graf Spee
segments.body: The German minister asked the owner of Montevideo's principal dockyard to devote the facility to Graf Spee, offering whatever payment he required. The dockyard belonged to a family understood to be of French descent. Its owner refused the request and, when asked whether his French background explained that decision, answered that he was acting as a Uruguayan. The refusal left the German cruiser without the principal local facility it wanted for repairs.

evidence.note: The German minister requested Montevideo's principal dockyard for Graf Spee, but its owner refused on the grounds of his Uruguayan allegiance.

segments.summary: The owner of Montevideo's main dockyard rejected a German request to devote the facility to Graf Spee despite an offer of generous payment.

segments.title: Millington-Drake's public diplomacy shapes Uruguay's response
segments.body: German officials regarded Eugen Millington-Drake as the architect of the resistance they met in Uruguay. He was a visible and popular public figure who worked far beyond private diplomatic meetings. Participation in sporting life and advocacy for Uruguay on the international stage had built goodwill and access before the crisis. Those years of public engagement helped shape the environment in which Uruguay handled a damaged belligerent warship.

evidence.note: German hostility toward Millington-Drake reflected the influence he had built through his popularity, sporting presence, and international advocacy for Uruguay.

segments.summary: German officials blamed Britain's popular ambassador for the Uruguayan resistance that frustrated Graf Spee.

segments.title: Graf Spee turns to improvised labor and Argentinian tugboats
segments.body: Graf Spee had little professional repair support in Montevideo. The Germans relied on Argentinian tugboats, crews from merchant ships, the cruiser's own sailors, and volunteers from Uruguay's German expatriate community. This was an improvised labor pool rather than the professional dockyard support the ship wanted. The stated need to restore seaworthiness remains questionable because Graf Spee had already steamed about 300 miles at nearly full speed after the battle.

evidence.note: Graf Spee relied on Argentinian tugboats, merchant sailors, her own crew, and German expatriate volunteers, while the stated need to restore seaworthiness remains questionable.

segments.summary: Denied professional local support, Graf Spee relied on tugboats, merchant sailors, her own crew, and German expatriate volunteers while the claimed need for repairs remained open to question.
